definition: Swing swaps and swing options are natural gas derivatives with daily delivery, distinct from standard futures/forwards/options that deliver over a full month; they are primarily used by utilities to manage volumetric risk.
core_idea: These instruments let a utility hedge the risk that customer gas usage deviates from expectations (e.g., a cold snap driving higher-than-forecast consumption), which matters especially when the utility cannot pass higher costs through to consumers.
key_points: Swing swap: exchanges a fixed price (set at the start of the delivery month) for the daily spot price reported by a pricing service.

Swing option: gives the buyer the right to purchase gas at a price set at the start of the delivery month (commonly referencing a survey such as Platts Inside FERC/IFERC) at any point during that month; these options typically limit how many times the buyer can exercise.
Both differ from standard swaps/options because the fixed reference price is set at the start of the delivery month rather than negotiated at the time of the trade.
Volumetric risk is the risk that a utility's customers use more (or less) gas than expected.
relationships: Reference price for the fixed leg comes from bidweek surveys
Similarly named but distinct from physical swing trades
trading_implications: Utilities use these instruments to hedge daily consumption variability without predicting exact usage in advance.
caveats: "Swing swap/option" (financial derivative, daily delivery, monthly fixed reference price) is distinct from a "swing trade" (physical storage arbitrage).
